 AI-powered cosmetic advertising in Ho Chi Minh City sparks debate.
 A studio in Ho Chi Minh City only takes 6 hours to create an AI-powered advertising video, instead of the 3-5 weeks required by the traditional process. But the more perfect the image, the more hesitant consumers are to spend money.
 ZNews • 14/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 
 In mid-October, tracislab, a creative AI- powered production studio based in Ho Chi Minh City, posted a simulated cosmetics advertisement video for the Korean brand RoundLab. 
 This is a video excerpt showcasing a concept design based on a Korean skincare product, created by an AI-powered creative studio in Ho Chi Minh City. Photo: Provided by the studio .
 The video received many comments praising its image quality and the potential application of AI in advertising production. However, some viewers questioned whether the AI-generated images accurately reflected the actual product.
 One comment, which received over 450 likes, read: “If I see any products advertised by your company, I won’t buy them. Thanks for letting me know about AI-powered cosmetic advertising.” Several other accounts expressed agreement. In fact, this was just a design concept from the studio, not a product actually produced under contract with RoundLab.
 This case reflects an increasingly important challenge as AI becomes more deeply involved in the advertising industry. The technology helps agencies shorten timelines, save costs, and expand creative possibilities. But for industries where visuals directly influence purchasing decisions, such as cosmetics, another question arises: do products still resemble what consumers see on the screen?
 AI shortens the production process.
 Speaking to Tri Thức - Znews , Tracy Nguyen, founder of tracislab, said the company is not overly concerned about the negative reactions, understanding that consumers still need time to get used to and accept AI-powered advertising.
 However, the studio still chose to pursue this direction, hoping to capitalize on the wave of AI applications in the creative and advertising production industry. According to the studio, the technology not only helps shorten time and optimize budgets but also opens up new approaches in commercial image production.
 Tracy Nguyen stated that the RoundLab commercial mockup video was completed in approximately 6 hours. This figure represents a significant difference compared to the traditional advertising production process, which can take 3-5 weeks.
 By combining AI with editing and post-production techniques, several processes can be streamlined. Production teams can experiment with multiple options for setting, lighting, motion, or composition without needing to hold a separate shoot for each concept. Studio representatives estimate that this approach optimizes production costs by approximately 60-70%.
 This shift isn't limited to just one agency. The Interactive Advertising Association's (IAB) report, The AI ​​Ad Gap Widens , published in January 2026, indicates that 83% of surveyed advertising leaders are using AI in their creative processes, up from 60% in 2024. Among ad buyers, 86% have already used or plan to use AI for video production. Cost optimization is one of the most frequently cited reasons, with 64% of respondents choosing it. 
 In March 2025, the cosmetics brand Too Faced launched a promotional campaign for its mascara line. The entire process, from concept to launch, took only 3 weeks thanks to AI.
 Major cosmetics brands are also experimenting with AI in various stages of advertising. Too Faced, a brand owned by Estée Lauder Companies, used both generative and agent-generated AI to produce much of its advertising campaign for Ribbon Wrapped Lash mascara. Meanwhile, parent company Estée Lauder Companies partnered with Adobe to use Firefly to expand and adapt imagery for a variety of digital advertising formats.
 You may also like In another direction, L'Oréal developed its CreAItech content creation department, using AI-generated imagery to produce campaign visuals, while adhering to the principle of not using AI-generated images of faces, bodies, hair, and skin that look realistic to illustrate or enhance product effectiveness.
 However, efficiency in terms of time and cost is not enough to assess the quality of an advertising product, especially when the images must also accurately convey the characteristics of the goods.
 With cosmetics, the color of lipstick, the shine of cream, the texture of serum, or the product's appearance on the skin can all influence buyer expectations. A beautiful image that misrepresents these characteristics can lead consumers to have a false impression of the product before placing an order.
 According to Tracy Nguyen, this is also why the company doesn't let AI recreate cosmetic products from scratch. For packaging, logos, colors, and textures, the team uses data from real products to perform 3D scans or recreate them based on the original data. AI primarily handles the background and surrounding effects such as lighting, water droplets, or fabric movement.
 The images are then manually checked and processed. A representative from the company stated that during the process, the AI ​​sometimes created errors such as distorted logos, incorrect fonts, or the appearance of non-existent characters on the packaging. To mitigate this, the team separates the text and logo, using vector data, 3D models, or high-resolution product images for post-processing.
 Therefore, AI does not replace the entire production process but is used in stages that can be automated. Identifying ideas, selecting visual options, and controlling final quality are still handled by humans. 
 In cosmetics and fashion , even a slight discrepancy in color, texture, or material can erode trust in advertising and the brand. (Illustrative image: Phuong Lam) 
 False expectations from a perfect image
 Whether produced using cameras or AI, the core issue of advertising remains the gap between what viewers see and the product they receive. With cosmetics, differences in color, texture, or coverage can mean the actual experience doesn't meet the expectations created by the advertising images.
 Minh Trang (28 years old, Cau Giay Ward, Hanoi ) said that the increasing use of AI in advertising has made her more aware of the gap between online images and actual products. When buying cosmetics online, she often carefully observes the cream's texture, shine, color, and absorption into the skin through advertising images and videos.
 Trang once bought a cream after seeing images that showed a thin, smooth, easy-to-spread, and fast-absorbing texture. However, the actual product was thicker and felt heavy on her skin. This experience wasn't related to an advertisement identified as using AI, but it made her more cautious about images that are too perfectly processed.
 "I'm not against using AI for backgrounds or effects, but product images need to be close to reality. For example, I want to clearly see the texture of the cream under normal lighting and know what the lipstick color will look like on the lips in reality," Trang told Tri Thức - Znews. 
 Minh Trang has been disappointed many times after ordering products because she trusted the advertisements. Photo: Provided by the interviewee. 
 Not only buyers, but also business owners have reason to care about the accuracy of advertising images. Ha Anh (33 years old, Xuan Hoa Ward, Ho Chi Minh City), the owner of a small sportswear shop on TikTok, used to use AI-powered video production services to introduce her products to customers.
 You may also like "If the product images are inaccurate in terms of color, style, or material, customers will have unrealistic expectations. When the received item doesn't match the picture, the shop not only has to handle exchanges and returns but also loses customer trust," Ha Anh said.
 Concerns about the authenticity of advertising arise as consumers have more ways to verify information before making a purchase. Images and videos still help them visualize products, but they are no longer the sole source of information.
 A Q&Me survey of 200 AI users aged 20-49 in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, titled "How Vietnamese use AI for shopping," revealed that 62% regularly or always use AI to research before making a purchase. However, only 15% are willing to buy immediately based on AI suggestions. Meanwhile, 60% continue to check information on e-commerce platforms like Shopee or Lazada, and 55% read reviews from other buyers.
 This result shows that consumers tend to compare information from multiple sources rather than relying solely on an initial advertisement or suggestion. For cosmetics, they might continue searching for product images under normal usage conditions, check reviews of the texture, or refer to the experiences of previous buyers.
 As AI makes advertising images more visually appealing and easier to refine, the need for transparency also becomes crucial. Agencies need to control the generated details, while brands must ensure that the images presented to buyers do not misrepresent the actual attributes of the product.
